Name: Lake Louise Summer Gondola Guide: Hikes, Tickets & Tips
Post Body:
The Lake Louise Summer Gondola & Hiking: Your Ultimate Guide

‍

‍

Quick answer: The Lake Louise Summer Gondola is a sightseeing lift at the Lake Louise Ski Resort that carries you up Whitehorn Mountain to 2,101 metres (6,893 feet) for wide views over Lake Louise, the Victoria Glacier and the peaks of the Great Divide. It runs daily from early June to Thanksgiving weekend in October, usually 9:00 am to 4:30 pm. An adult ticket at the window was $65 CAD in 2026, with 10% off when you buy online. At the top you will find short alpine hiking trails, a free Wildlife Interpretive Centre and some of the best odds in the Canadian Rockies of seeing a wild grizzly bear from a safe distance.

‍

That is the short version. This guide covers everything else you need to plan a great day: what the ride is actually like, whether to choose the open chairlift or the enclosed gondola, which trails to hike at the top, how bear viewing works, where to park, and how to fit the gondola into a bigger day of Lake Louise sightseeing. Our guides at Vista Chase spend most summer days driving guests around Lake Louise, so the advice here comes from what we see on the ground every season.

‍

What Is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola?

‍

Most people know the Lake Louise Ski Resort as one of the biggest ski hills in Canada. Once the snow melts, the same lift line turns into one of the easiest ways to reach the alpine in Banff National Park. The Lake Louise Gondola climbs the south face of Whitehorn Mountain, directly across the valley from Lake Louise itself. That position is the whole point. Instead of standing at the lakeshore looking up, you look down on the turquoise water, the Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise and the glaciers behind them from above.

‍

The ride takes around 14 minutes each way. Below you is the Whitehorn wildlife corridor, a protected stretch of slope where grizzly bears, black bears, elk and deer feed through the summer. At the summit there is a viewing deck, a network of short hiking trails, and food and drink options at the base and mid mountain. You can ride as often as you like on the same day, because a ticket covers unlimited rides for one day.

‍

Is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola Worth It?

‍

For most visitors, yes. Here is why the Lake Louise Summer Gondola earns a spot on a Banff itinerary:

‍

  • The view is different from anything at the lake. You see Lake Louise, Mount Temple, the Victoria Glacier and the Bow Valley all at once, which you cannot do from the shoreline.
  • It is the easiest way into the alpine. You reach 2,101 metres without a long climb, which makes it ideal for families, older travellers and anyone short on time.
  • Wildlife odds are excellent. The resort is well known as one of the best places in the Rockies to see grizzly bears safely, and sightings from the chairs are common in summer.
  • It is quieter than the big name stops. While the Lake Louise lakeshore fills up by mid morning, the gondola rarely feels as crowded.
  • Parking is free. That alone saves real money and stress compared to the lakeshore lot.

‍

Who might skip it? Experienced hikers with only one day at Lake Louise may prefer to spend their legs on the Lake Agnes Teahouse or the Plain of Six Glaciers instead. If you have two days, do both.

‍

Lake Louise Summer Gondola Tickets and Hours

‍

Ticket prices

‍

Ticket prices change each season, so always confirm on the Lake Louise Ski Resort website before you go. As a guide, these were the 2026 window prices for an all day Lake Louise Summer Gondola ticket in Canadian dollars:

‍

  • Adult (18 to 64): $65
  • Senior (65 and over): $54
  • Youth (13 to 17): $29
  • Child (6 to 12): $16
  • Ages 5 and under: free

‍

Buying online in advance saves 10% off the window price. You then scan the QR code from your receipt at a ticket pickup box or visit Guest Services. Bow Valley residents and Plus+Card holders get bigger discounts. Tickets are non refundable, non transferable and valid for unlimited rides on the day you use

them.

‍

Combo tickets with the lakeshore shuttle

‍

The resort also sells packages that bundle the gondola with its own shuttle to the Lake Louise lakeshore, and in some periods to Moraine Lake as well. In 2026 the Gondola plus Lake Louise Shuttle package was $94 for adults, and the two lake package with Moraine Lake was $159 for adults. Combo sales are final.

Note that the Moraine Lake portion has been listed as temporarily unavailable at times, so check availability when you book.

‍

Operating hours and season

‍

The 2026 season ran daily from June 5 to Thanksgiving weekend in October, with the lift open from 9:00 am to 4:30 pm and the last ride down at about 5:10 pm. Earlier seasons stayed open later in July and August, so hours can shift year to year. The lift can also pause for high winds or lightning, which is common

on hot afternoons in the Rockies. Expect the next season to open in early June again and confirm exact dates in spring.
‍
Planning your Moraine Lake visit? Start with our first-timer’s guide to the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail for access rules, timing and what to bring.

‍

Gondola or Chairlift: Choosing Your Ride Up Whitehorn Mountain

‍

The lift line carries both enclosed gondola cabins and open chairs, and you choose which one to board. Each feels very different.

‍

  • Enclosed gondola: Sheltered from wind and rain, easy for young children, and the better pick on a cold or wet day. Children under 42 inches (106 cm) must ride in an enclosed gondola with an adult.
  • Open Lake Louise chairlift: Quieter, with nothing between you and the mountain air. Many guests say they spot more wildlife from the open chairs because sound and sightlines are better.

‍

A favourite local trick is to ride up in a gondola and come down on a chair. Heading down, you face the valley the whole way, so the views over Lake Louise are at their widest. Children under 12 must ride with at least one adult either way, and pets are not allowed on the lift apart from service animals.

‍

Best Hiking Trails from the Lake Louise Summer Gondola

‍

The trails at the top are short, scenic and well marked, with round trips of roughly 1.7 to 2.5 km. They suit beginners and families, but you are still at over 2,000 metres in real mountain terrain, so treat them with respect.

‍

Kicking Horse Pass Viewpoint Trail

‍

This is the trail most visitors walk, and it is the best introduction to Canadian Rockies hiking from the top of the lift. It is about 1.7 km return and heads west from the summit through wildflower meadows before entering a larch forest. It ends at a viewpoint around 2,185 metres looking toward Kicking Horse Pass and

the Continental Divide. In July and August the meadows are full of wildflowers. In the last two weeks of September the larches turn gold, which makes this one of the easiest larch walks in Banff National Park.

‍

Pika Trail

‍

The Pika Trail heads east from the summit and is about 2.5 km return, climbing to roughly 2,276 metres. It is a little steeper and quieter than the Kicking Horse route, with rocky slopes where you may hear the sharp whistle of pikas and hoary marmots. In some seasons it has connected to a longer viewpoint over

the Ptarmigan Valley when conditions allow.

‍

Guided interpretive walks

‍

In many summers the resort has offered guided walks with interpretive staff who explain bear behaviour, alpine plants and the history of the wildlife corridor. These walks are a great choice if you are travelling with kids or want context for what you are seeing. Ask at Guest Services on the day, since schedules

change with weather and trail conditions.

‍

Rules for hiking at the top

‍

Hiking on the Lake Louise Summer Gondola trails comes with rules that keep both people and bears safe:

‍

  • Hiking on the lower mountain is not allowed because it is an active wildlife corridor. You must ride the lift both up and down.
  • Trails can close at any time because of bear activity, weather or construction. Never enter a closed area.
  • The resort strongly recommends hiking in groups of four or more.
  • Carry bear spray where you can reach it quickly, and make noise on blind corners.

‍

Pairing the gondola with other Lake Louise hiking trails

‍

If you want a bigger hike, the gondola works well as a half day add on to the classic trails at the lake. A popular plan is the Lake Agnes Teahouse in the morning and the gondola in the afternoon when your legs need a rest. For distances, difficulty and timing on every major route, from the Lakeshore Trail to the Big

Beehive and the Teahouse Loop, read our complete Lake Louise hiking guide.

‍

Wildlife Viewing at Lake Louise: Can You See Grizzly Bears?

‍

Yes, and this is the reason many people ride the Lake Louise Gondola in the first place. The slopes under the lift sit inside a protected corridor where grizzly bears feed on grasses, dandelions, clover and, later in summer, buffaloberries. Because people stay on the lift and the hiking is limited to the upper mountain,

bears can feed in the open while visitors watch from above. The resort lists grizzly bears, black bears, lynx, moose, mountain goats, elk and deer among the species seen here.

‍

A few tips to improve your chances:

‍

  • Ride early in the day or in the late afternoon, when bears are usually more active.
  • Choose an open chair, stay quiet and scan the clearings and slope edges below you.
  • Bring binoculars or a camera with a zoom lens. Bears are often a long way down the slope.
  • Ask the lift staff. They often know where a bear has been feeding that day.

‍

No sighting is ever guaranteed in the wild, and that is part of what makes it special when it happens. If wildlife is a big part of your trip, our guide to wildlife viewing tours in Banff covers the best seasons, species and other hotspots across the park.

‍

Food, Facilities and the Wildlife Interpretive Centre

‍

You will not go hungry. At the base, the Lodge of the Ten Peaks has a cafeteria for breakfast and lunch, plus Slopeside Coffee for a hot drink before the ride. Mid mountain, at around 6,700 feet, the Whitehorn Bistro has a patio with one of the best lunch views in Banff National Park. The resort also sells Gondola

and Dining combos that bundle your ride with a meal.

‍

Do not skip the complimentary Wildlife Interpretive Centre. It explains the bears, plants and ecosystems you are looking at, and kids especially love it. There is also a gift shop for souvenirs and essentials. The resort is not fully wheelchair accessible, so check its accessibility information before your visit if that

matters for your group.

‍

Lake Louise Summer Gondola vs Banff Summer Gondola

‍

Visitors often ask whether they should ride the Lake Louise Summer Gondola or one of the gondolas near Banff town. They are very different experiences.

‍

  • Lake Louise Summer Gondola: Seasonal, quieter, free parking, open chair or enclosed cabin, and the strongest odds of wildlife sightings. The highlight is the view across to Lake Louise and its glaciers.
  • Banff Gondola on Sulphur Mountain: Right next to Banff town, open year round, with enclosed cabins, restaurants and a long summit boardwalk. It is busier but very convenient if you are staying in Banff.
  • Banff Sunshine Summer Gondola: Banff's largest gondola, rising from about 1,659 to 2,159 metres in eight passenger cabins, with a chairlift ride included. It opened on July 6 for the 2026 summer season and gives access to the alpine meadows of Sunshine Village.

‍

If you are basing yourself in Lake Louise or want wildlife, choose Lake Louise. If you only have a few hours in Banff town, Sulphur Mountain is the easier fit. Many visitors on longer trips ride both.

‍

How to Get to the Lake Louise Summer Gondola

‍

The gondola is at the Lake Louise Ski Resort, 1 Whitehorn Road, about a five minute drive from Lake Louise Village and roughly 45 minutes from Banff town. Unlike the Lake Louise lakeshore, where parking cost $42 per vehicle per day in 2026 and the lot often fills early, the ski resort has large free lots for cars and RVs.

‍

The ski resort area is also where the Parks Canada Park and Ride for the Lake Louise and Moraine Lake shuttles operates in summer, so it is easy to combine the gondola with a shuttle to the lakes. Remember that you need a valid Parks Canada pass to be anywhere in Banff National Park, including the ski resort.

The pass is separate from your gondola ticket.

‍

Best Time to Visit Lake Louise in Summer

‍

The best time to visit Lake Louise in summer depends on what you want to see.

‍

  • June: The lift opens and bears are often feeding low on the slopes. Upper trails may still hold patches of snow, and the lake itself can still be thawing early in the month.
  • July and August: Peak summer in Banff National Park. Wildflowers fill the alpine meadows, all trails are usually open and the weather is warmest. It is also the busiest period, so start early.
  • Mid to late September: Our favourite time. The crowds ease, the air is crisp and the larches on the Kicking Horse Pass Viewpoint Trail turn gold, usually peaking in the last week of the month.
  • Early October: The final weeks before the lift closes on Thanksgiving weekend. Cold mornings and a chance of early snow, but very quiet.

‍

For time of day, mornings are usually calmer and clearer, while afternoons on hot days can bring thunderstorms that pause the lift.

‍

What to Bring for Hiking at Lake Louise

‍

The temperature at the top can be 10 degrees colder than in the parking lot, and mountain weather changes fast. Pack for the summit, not the base.

‍

  • A warm mid layer and a waterproof, windproof jacket, even in August
  • Sturdy shoes with good grip for rocky, sometimes muddy trails
  • Bear spray carried on your hip or chest strap
  • Water and snacks, especially if you plan to hike both trails
  • Sunscreen, sunglasses and a hat, since UV is stronger at altitude
  • Binoculars or a zoom lens for wildlife viewing
  • Gloves and a toque in September and October

‍

For a full list by season, see our guide to things to pack for Banff weather.

‍

Is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola Family Friendly?

‍

It is one of the most family friendly Lake Louise summer activities. Children 5 and under ride free, youth and child tickets are heavily discounted, and the enclosed gondolas feel safe for nervous little ones. The trails at the top are short enough for most school age kids, the Wildlife Interpretive Centre keeps curious

minds busy, and the chance of seeing a real grizzly bear tends to be the highlight of the trip for children. Just remember that kids under 12 must ride with an adult, and those under 42 inches must ride in an enclosed cabin.

‍

How Long Should You Spend at the Lake Louise Summer Gondola?

‍

Plan on two to three hours for a relaxed visit. That gives you about 30 minutes of riding in total, time on the viewing deck, one trail at the top and a coffee or snack. If you want to hike both trails, stop for lunch at the Whitehorn Bistro and spend time in the Interpretive Centre, allow four hours or more.

‍

Here is how the gondola fits into a full day of Lake Louise sightseeing:

  • Early morning: Lake Louise lakeshore before the crowds, with a walk along the Lakeshore Trail or a climb to Fairview Lookout.
  • Late morning: Lake Agnes Teahouse hike for those who want a bigger climb.
  • Lunch: Lake Louise Village or the Whitehorn Bistro.
  • Afternoon: Ride the Lake Louise Summer Gondola, hike the Kicking Horse Pass Viewpoint Trail and watch for bears on the way down.

‍

Things to Do at Lake Louise in Summer Beyond the Gondola

‍

The gondola is one piece of a bigger picture. Other things to do at Lake Louise in summer include canoeing on the lake, hiking to the two historic teahouses, walking the Plain of Six Glaciers toward the Victoria Glacier, and taking the short trip to Moraine Lake for the famous Rockpile viewpoint over the Valley of the

Ten Peaks.

‍

The hardest part is usually getting there, since parking at the lakes is limited and Moraine Lake Road is closed to private vehicles. Our full day shuttle to Lake Louise and Moraine Lake solves that, with pickup in Canmore, Banff and Lake Louise Village, Parks Canada entry included, a local guide, a maximum of 12

guests, and about four hours at Lake Louise plus three at Moraine Lake. If the gondola is a must for your group, ask us about a private tour so we can build the ride and the Whitehorn trails into your day.

‍

Frequently Asked Questions About the Lake Louise Summer Gondola

‍

What is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola?

‍

The Lake Louise Summer Gondola is a sightseeing lift at the Lake Louise Ski Resort in Banff National Park. It carries visitors up Whitehorn Mountain to 2,101 metres in either an enclosed gondola or an open chair, with views over Lake Louise and the surrounding glaciers, short hiking trails at the top and frequent wildlife sightings.

‍

Is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola worth visiting?

‍

Yes. It offers a view of Lake Louise you cannot get from the shore, easy access to alpine trails, free parking and some of the best grizzly bear viewing in the Canadian Rockies. It is especially worth it for families, first time visitors and anyone who wants mountain views without a long hike.

‍

How much do Lake Louise Summer Gondola tickets cost?

‍

In 2026 an all day adult ticket was $65 CAD at the window, seniors were $54, youth were $29, children aged 6 to 12 were $16, and kids 5 and under rode free. Buying online saves 10%. Prices are set each season, so check the resort website for current rates.

‍

What are the operating hours of the Lake Louise Summer Gondola?

‍

In 2026 the gondola ran daily from June 5 to Thanksgiving weekend in October, from 9:00 am to 4:30 pm, with the last ride down around 5:10 pm. Hours can change by season and the lift may pause for wind or lightning.

‍

What hiking trails can you access from the Summer Gondola?

‍

The main trails from the top are the Kicking Horse Pass Viewpoint Trail, about 1.7 km return, and the Pika Trail, about 2.5 km return. Both are short alpine walks with big views. Hiking on the lower mountain is not permitted, so you must ride the lift back down.

‍

Can you see grizzly bears from the Lake Louise Gondola?

‍

Yes. The slopes below the lift are part of a protected wildlife corridor, and grizzly bears are often seen feeding there in summer. Black bears, elk, deer and other wildlife are also spotted. Sightings are common but never guaranteed.

‍

What should I bring for hiking at Lake Louise?

‍

Bring a warm layer, a waterproof jacket, sturdy shoes, bear spray, water, snacks, sunscreen and sunglasses. Binoculars help with wildlife viewing. In September and October add gloves and a toque, since temperatures at the top can be close to freezing.

‍

Is the Lake Louise Summer Gondola family friendly?

‍

Yes. Kids 5 and under ride free, the enclosed cabins suit young children, the trails at the top are short, and the free Wildlife Interpretive Centre is great for curious kids. Children under 12 must ride with an adult.

‍

When is the best time to visit Lake Louise in summer?

‍

July and August bring wildflowers, open trails and the warmest weather, while mid to late September offers fewer crowds and golden larches. For the gondola, early morning and late afternoon give the best chances of seeing wildlife.

‍

How long should I spend at the Lake Louise Summer Gondola?

‍

Most visitors spend two to three hours, which covers the ride, the viewing deck and one short trail. Allow four hours or more if you want to hike both trails, eat at the Whitehorn Bistro and visit the Interpretive Centre.

‍

Plan Your Lake Louise Summer Day

‍

The Lake Louise Summer Gondola is one of those rare experiences that works for almost everyone: the views are huge, the effort is low and there is always a chance of watching a grizzly bear go about its day. Book your tickets online, ride early or late, carry bear spray, and pair it with a morning at the lakeshore. Get those pieces right and you will see Lake Louise from every angle in a single summer day.

‍
Post Summary: Plan your Lake Louise Summer Gondola trip: ticket prices, hours, the best hiking trails from the top, grizzly bear viewing tips and what to pack.

Name: Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse Hike: Local Guide from Lake Louise
Post Body:
Hiking to the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse from Lake Louise: A Local's Guide

‍

‍

Most people who visit Lake Louise stand on the shoreline, photograph the Victoria Glacier at the far end of the lake, and leave. The glacier stays a backdrop. Walk to the end of the lake and keep going, though, and something changes. The crowds thin out, the trail climbs onto old glacial moraine, and about two

hours later you are sitting on the porch of a stone teahouse with ice fields hanging off the cliffs above you.

‍

That walk is the Plain of Six Glaciers hike, and it is one of the best half day outings in Banff National Park. Our guides at Vista Chase drop hikers at the Lake Louise trailhead most days of the summer, so this guide covers what we actually tell people: how long it takes, what the trail is like, what to expect at the

teahouse, and how to plan the day so it goes smoothly.

‍

Quick Answer: How Long Is the Plain of Six Glaciers Hike?

‍

The Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse is about 5.5 km one way from the Lake Louise lakeshore, with roughly 365 metres of elevation gain. Most hikers reach it in 1.5 to 2.5 hours, and the full round trip with a teahouse stop takes about 4 to 5 hours. If you continue past the teahouse to the Abbot Pass viewpoint, add

another 1 to 2 hours.

‍

Plain of Six Glaciers Trail at a Glance

‍

  • Trailhead: Lake Louise lakeshore, in front of the Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise
  • Distance to the teahouse: about 5.5 km one way, or 11 km return
  • Distance to the end viewpoint: roughly another 1 to 1.5 km past the teahouse
  • Elevation gain to the teahouse: about 365 metres
  • Difficulty: moderate, with two steep sets of switchbacks near the top
  • Time: 4 to 5 hours return with a break, 5 to 6 hours with the viewpoint
  • Teahouse season: usually early June to mid October, depending on snow
  • Payment at the teahouse: bring Canadian cash
  • Dogs: allowed on a leash
  • Reservations: none needed for the trail or the teahouse

‍

Why the Plain of Six Glaciers Hike Is Worth Your Day

‍

Lake Louise has two famous teahouse hikes, and most first time visitors pick Lake Agnes because it is shorter. The Plain of Six Glaciers trail rewards the extra distance in a different way. Instead of ending at a pretty alpine lake, it takes you into the glacial valley that feeds Lake Louise. You walk beside the ice rather

than looking at it from across the water.

‍

The grade is gentler than the Lake Agnes trail for most of the way, the crowds drop off sharply after the first 2 km, and on warm afternoons you can hear chunks of ice breaking off the hanging glaciers across the valley. It feels much more remote than it actually is.

‍

A Short History of the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse

‍

The teahouse was built by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the mid 1920s. The idea came from the Swiss mountain guides the CPR employed at Lake Louise, who wanted a rest stop for guests heading up toward Abbot Pass and the climbing routes on Mount Victoria and Mount Lefroy. The main building is two

storeys of stone with wooden verandas, and a few small cabins were added nearby in the late 1920s. Today those cabins house staff.

‍

The same family has run the teahouse since 1959. There is still no electricity and no road. Cooking is done on propane, dry goods come in by helicopter, and fresh supplies arrive by horse or on the backs of staff who hike up and stay for days at a time. Keep that in mind when you see the prices and the menu.

Everything you eat there made the same trip you just did.

‍

The name refers to the glaciers that surround the valley, including the Upper and Lower Victoria glaciers, the Upper and Lower Lefroy glaciers, and the glaciers on Mount Aberdeen and Popes Peak. Not all six are equally obvious from the teahouse, which is part of the reason to walk on to the viewpoint.

‍

How to Get to the Plain of Six Glaciers Trailhead

‍

The trail starts at the Lake Louise lakeshore, about 45 minutes from Banff by road. Getting there is usually the hardest part of the day.

‍

The Lake Louise Lakeshore parking lot is paid from mid May to mid October, at $42 per vehicle per day in 2026, and on summer mornings it is often full before most visitors have finished breakfast. Once it fills, traffic staff turn cars away at the bottom of the hill. Your other options are the Parks Canada shuttle from

the Lake Louise Park and Ride, which needs an advance reservation, and Roam Transit from Banff.

‍

If you would rather not juggle reservations and timing, our Lake Louise and Moraine Lake shuttles pick up in Canmore, Banff and Lake Louise Village. The Day Shuttle gives you 3 to 4 hours at each lake, which is enough to reach the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse and back at a steady pace. It is tight if you also

want the viewpoint beyond the teahouse, so for a longer hike a private tour lets us build the whole day around your time on the trail.

‍

You also need a valid Parks Canada pass for any hike in Banff National Park. The pass is separate from parking and shuttle fees.

‍

The Plain of Six Glaciers Trail, Section by Section

‍

Section 1: The Lakeshore (0 to 2 km)

‍

Start in front of the Chateau and follow the wide path along the north shore of Lake Louise. Within a few hundred metres you will pass the junction for Lake Agnes on your right. Stay on the lakeshore. This stretch is flat and busy near the hotel, then quiets down as you go. Look up at the cliffs on your right and you

will often spot rock climbers on the quartzite walls.

‍

At the far end of the lake, the path crosses silty flats where meltwater streams braid their way into the lake. This is where the water gets its colour, from fine rock flour ground off the glaciers ahead of you.

‍

Section 2: Into the Valley (2 to 4 km)

‍

Past the end of the lake the trail starts to climb, gently at first, through forest and across a few open avalanche paths. The views open up behind you over the lake and ahead toward the Victoria Glacier. Partway along, the Highline Trail joins from the right. That is the connector hikers use to link the two teahouses into one loop.

‍

Section 3: Switchbacks to the Teahouse (4 to 5.5 km)

‍

The last section is where most of the climbing happens. Two sets of tight switchbacks lead up through the trees, and they are steeper than anything earlier on the trail. Take them slowly. When the trail flattens and you see the stone building with its verandas, you have arrived. The teahouse sits at around 2,100

metres, so you may feel the altitude a little if you have just flown in from sea level.

‍

Section 4: Beyond the Teahouse to the Abbot Pass Viewpoint

‍

Many people stop at the teahouse, and that is a perfectly good day. If you have the time and energy, keep going. The trail continues roughly another 1 to 1.5 km along the crest of a lateral moraine to a viewpoint facing the Victoria Glacier, Mount Lefroy and the notch of Abbot Pass. The gully below the pass is

known locally as the Death Trap because of the ice and rock that fall into it, and from here you can see why.

‍

This last part is rougher, narrower and more exposed than the trail below. Watch your footing on the loose rock, and do not walk out onto the glacier or the snow slopes below it. The viewpoint is the end of the hiking trail. Anything past it is mountaineering terrain.

‍

What to Expect at the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse

‍

The teahouse serves loose leaf tea, coffee, homemade soups, sandwiches, tea biscuits and baked goods. The chocolate cake has a loyal following. Portions are simple and honest rather than fancy, and that suits the setting.

‍

Plan on paying with cash. The teahouse runs without electricity and is best treated as cash only, so bring Canadian dollars in small bills. Hours are roughly morning to late afternoon in season, and the kitchen can wind down before closing, so aim to arrive by early afternoon if lunch is part of your plan.

‍

Seating is on the verandas and at a few outdoor tables. It is generally easier to find a seat here than at Lake Agnes, especially on weekdays. There is an outhouse near the teahouse but no garbage service on the trail, so pack out everything you bring. Please do not feed the chipmunks or the grey jays, however

bold they get.

‍

Plain of Six Glaciers vs Lake Agnes Teahouse: Which One Should You Hike?

‍

If you only have time for one, here is how we usually help guests decide. Lake Agnes is about 7 km return with roughly 400 metres of climbing, so it is shorter but steeper, and it ends beside an alpine lake. It is also much busier, with queues at the teahouse by late morning in summer. The Plain of Six Glaciers is

about 11 km return with a gentler grade, quieter trails and closer views of the glaciers, but no lake at the top.

‍

Choose Lake Agnes if you are short on time or want the classic Lake Louise viewpoint from the Big Beehive. Choose the Plain of Six Glaciers if you want glaciers up close and fewer people. Strong hikers can do both in one day on the Teahouse Loop, which links them via the Highline Trail in about 14.6 km. Our

‍Lake Louise hiking guide covers that loop and every other major trail around the lake, and if you want a bigger challenge above Lake Agnes, read our local's guide to hiking the Devil's Thumb before you commit.

‍

Best Time to Hike the Plain of Six Glaciers

‍

The teahouse usually opens in early June and closes in mid October, but the trail itself has a narrower sweet spot.

‍

  • June: The lower trail is usually clear, but the upper section and the route beyond the teahouse can still hold snow, and avalanche paths may not have fully released. Carry microspikes and turn around if the trail disappears under snow.
  • July and August: Peak season. The full trail is open, the lake is at its most vivid colour, and the trail is busy. Start before 8 am for a quieter walk and to stay ahead of afternoon thunderstorms.
  • September to early October: Our favourite window. Fewer people, crisp air and clear views, though mornings can be below freezing and an early snowfall can close the upper trail for a few days.
  • Mid October to May: The teahouse is closed and the trail beyond the lake crosses avalanche terrain. Unless you have avalanche training and gear, stick to the lakeshore.

‍

What to Pack for the Plain of Six Glaciers Hike

‍

  • Sturdy hiking shoes or boots with good grip, especially for the rocky section past the teahouse
  • A waterproof jacket and a warm layer, even in August
  • Bear spray, carried on your hip or chest strap where you can reach it quickly
  • At least 1.5 to 2 litres of water per person, since there is no drinking water on the trail
  • Snacks, even if you plan to eat at the teahouse
  • Sunscreen, sunglasses and a hat for the open moraine near the top
  • Canadian cash for the teahouse
  • An offline trail map and a small power bank, since mobile signal is patchy on the upper trail
  • Microspikes in June, late September and October

‍

Safety on the Trail

‍

This is grizzly and black bear country. Make noise on blind corners and near rushing water, keep children close, and never leave food or wrappers behind. Parks Canada sometimes posts warnings, group size rules or temporary closures in the Lake Louise area during periods of high bear activity, so check the trail

conditions report on the morning of your hike.

‍

Mountain weather changes quickly, and thunderstorms build over the peaks on hot afternoons. If you hear thunder, head down. Past the teahouse, the main hazards are loose rock and the temptation to get closer to the ice. Stay on the trail, keep your distance from the glacier, and remember that the descent on

tired legs is where most slips happen.

‍

A Sample Plain of Six Glaciers Day

‍

  • 7:30 am: Arrive at the Lake Louise lakeshore and take your photos while the water is still calm
  • 8:00 am: Start walking along the lakeshore
  • 10:00 am: Reach the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse, order tea and something warm
  • 10:45 am: Continue to the Abbot Pass viewpoint
  • 11:45 am: Back at the teahouse for lunch if you skipped it earlier
  • 2:00 pm: Return to the lakeshore for a slow walk, a canoe, or a ride on to Moraine Lake

‍

Starting early is the single best thing you can do. You avoid the worst of the crowds on the lakeshore, you beat the afternoon weather, and you get a seat at the teahouse without waiting.

‍

Plan Your Lake Louise Hiking Day with Vista Chase

‍

The trail itself is straightforward. The hard part is usually everything before it: the parking, the reservations and the timing. That is what our team handles every day of the season. Whether you want a seat on a shared shuttle with enough time at Lake Louise to reach the teahouse, or a private day built around a

longer hike and a stop at Moraine Lake afterward, our local guides can point you to the right option and tell you which trails are clear that week.

‍

Frequently Asked Questions

‍

How long does it take to hike to the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse?

‍

Most hikers reach the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse in 1.5 to 2.5 hours from the Lake Louise lakeshore. The round trip, including a stop at the teahouse, usually takes 4 to 5 hours. Adding the Abbot Pass viewpoint beyond the teahouse brings the total to around 5 to 6 hours.

‍

How hard is the Plain of Six Glaciers hike?

‍

The Plain of Six Glaciers hike is moderate. It covers about 11 km return with roughly 365 metres of elevation gain. Most of the trail is a gentle climb, but two steep sets of switchbacks below the teahouse and the rocky section to the viewpoint are more demanding. Active adults who take breaks usually manage it

comfortably.

‍

Is the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse cash only?

‍

Plan on paying with cash. The teahouse has no electricity and is best treated as cash only, so bring Canadian dollars in small bills for tea, soup, sandwiches and baked goods. There is no ATM on the trail, so get cash before you leave Banff or Lake Louise Village.

‍

When is the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse open?

‍

The teahouse usually operates from early June to mid October, depending on snow conditions. During the season it is typically open from morning until late afternoon. Opening and closing dates change each year with the weather, so check before you go if a stop at the teahouse is the main goal of your hike.

‍

Do you need a reservation for the trail or the teahouse?

‍

No. You do not need a reservation to hike the Plain of Six Glaciers trail or to eat at the teahouse. You do need a valid Parks Canada pass, and you will need to plan your transport to Lake Louise in advance, because the lakeshore parking lot fills early and Parks Canada shuttles require reservations.

‍

Can kids do the Plain of Six Glaciers hike?

‍

Yes, many families complete the hike to the teahouse with school age children who are used to walking. The 11 km round trip is long for young kids, so build in plenty of breaks. The section beyond the teahouse is rockier and more exposed, and we would only take older, confident children there with close

supervision.

‍

Can you hike Lake Agnes and the Plain of Six Glaciers in one day?

‍

Yes. The Teahouse Loop links both teahouses using the Highline Trail and covers about 14.6 km in 5 to 6 hours for fit hikers. Most people hike up to Lake Agnes first while their legs are fresh, cross to the Plain of Six Glaciers, then finish with the gentle walk back along the lakeshore.

‍

Are dogs allowed on the Plain of Six Glaciers trail?

‍

Yes, dogs are allowed on the Plain of Six Glaciers trail as long as they are on a leash at all times, which is the rule throughout Banff National Park. Bring water for your dog and keep it close, since this is active bear habitat.

‍

Is there cell service on the Plain of Six Glaciers trail?

‍

There is some mobile signal at the Lake Louise lakeshore, but it becomes patchy and unreliable as you head up the valley toward the teahouse. Download an offline trail map before you start and tell someone your plan and expected return time.

‍

How do I get to Lake Louise for the hike without parking?

‍

You can take the Parks Canada shuttle from the Lake Louise Park and Ride with an advance reservation, ride Roam Transit from Banff, or book a shuttle or tour with a local operator. Vista Chase runs shuttles to Lake Louise and Moraine Lake with pickups in Canmore, Banff and Lake Louise Village, so you can skip

the parking lot entirely.

‍

Before You Go

‍

Check the Parks Canada trail report the morning of your hike, bring cash and layers, and start earlier than feels necessary. Do those three things and the Plain of Six Glaciers will give you one of the best days you can have at Lake Louise.

‍
Post Summary: Hike to the Plain of Six Glaciers Teahouse from Lake Louise: distance, time, trail notes, what to order, cash tips and how to skip the parking stress.

Name: Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail: First-Timer’s Guide & Tips
Post Body:
A First-Timer’s Guide to Visiting the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail
‍

‍
Quick Answer: What Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?
‍

The Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail is a very short, easy walk in Banff National Park that climbs a pile of ancient glacial rubble beside the lake and rewards you with the postcard view of Moraine Lake and the Valley of the Ten Peaks. Most visitors finish it in 10 to 20 minutes, it needs no hiking experience, and it is free to walk. The real challenge is not the trail itself but getting to Moraine Lake, because the road is closed to personal vehicles and access runs through the Parks Canada shuttle, licensed commercial operators or a guided tour.


If you are visiting for the first time, this guide covers where the trail is, how to reach it, how hard it is, the best time of day and year to go, what to pack and the mistakes that cost first-timers their best photos.


Where Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail Located?


Moraine Lake sits inside Banff National Park in Alberta, Canada, about 14 kilometres from Lake Louise Village at the end of Moraine Lake Road. The Rockpile Trail starts right at the lake’s edge, a short walk from the lakeside facilities and the canoe dock. You do not need to drive or hike to a remote trailhead. Once you step off your shuttle or tour vehicle, the signed path to the Rockpile is only moments away.
‍

The lake lies in the Valley of the Ten Peaks, a wall of jagged summits that rise above 3,000 metres. That mountain backdrop is the reason the Rockpile viewpoint is considered one of the most photographed vantage points in the Canadian Rockies.


Why the Rockpile Viewpoint Is So Famous


The Rockpile is a natural mound of boulders left behind by an ancient rockslide or glacial deposit. Climbing it lifts you high enough to see the full length of the lake, its famously vivid blue-green colour and the line of peaks behind it. Travellers often call it the Twenty Dollar View, because this scene appeared on the back of the Canadian twenty-dollar bill in the late twentieth century.


That history is part of the appeal, but the practical reason people love it is simple. You get one of the most dramatic mountain views in North America for a few minutes of easy walking.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail Suitable for Beginners?


Yes. The Rockpile Trail is one of the most beginner-friendly viewpoints in the Rockies. The path is short, and the climb is a brief set of steps and rocky footing rather than a sustained ascent. Families with school-age children, older travellers who are comfortable with steps and first-time visitors with no hiking gear can all manage it.
‍

A few honest caveats apply. The final section involves uneven rock and stairs, so it is not suitable for wheelchairs or strollers. Footing can be slippery after rain or in early-season frost. Moraine Lake sits at roughly 1,880 metres, so some visitors feel slightly breathless even on a short climb.


How Long Does It Take to Hike the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


Plan on about 10 to 20 minutes for the walk up and the same or less for the return. The trail itself is well under a kilometre round trip. What stretches the visit is everything around it: waiting for other visitors to clear the summit for a photo, taking in the view and walking the lakeshore afterwards.

For a comfortable first visit, set aside 20 to 30 minutes for the Rockpile alone. If you also want to explore the lakeshore, rent a canoe or enjoy a quiet moment at the water, allow 2 to 3 hours at Moraine Lake in total.


How Difficult Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


The trail is rated easy. The elevation gain is small, the surface is well established and there are no exposed ridges. The only thing that can change the experience is weather, because wet stone, snow or ice can make the upper steps tricky. Wear shoes with decent grip rather than flat-soled fashion shoes, and take your time on the descent when the summit is crowded.
‍

If you want a longer walk after the viewpoint, the flat lakeshore path along the water is a gentle extension, and stronger hikers can look at the longer trails that begin in the same valley. For more trail ideas nearby, read our Lake Louise hiking guide.


Can You Drive Directly to Moraine Lake?


No. Moraine Lake Road has been closed to personal vehicles year-round since 2023, with exceptions that cover licensed commercial operators, registered guests of Moraine Lake Lodge and certain official vehicles. The old routine of arriving before sunrise to claim a parking space no longer exists.

This single rule is why so many first-timers feel confused. They see the Rockpile in photos, assume they can drive up and then discover the road is closed. Our detailed Moraine Lake access rules and parking guide explains what is currently permitted so you can plan before you arrive.


Do You Need a Shuttle Reservation to Visit Moraine Lake?


It depends on how you travel. If you use the official Parks Canada shuttle from the Lake Louise Park and Ride, you need a reservation for a specific departure time, and popular dates sell out quickly after booking opens. In the 2026 season the Parks Canada shuttle was scheduled to run from June 1 to October 12, weather permitting, so it is important to confirm current operating dates on the Parks Canada website before you plan a late-season trip.
‍

If you travel with a licensed commercial operator or a guided tour, the operator handles the access, timing and logistics, so you do not need to compete for a public shuttle seat. That is the reason many travellers who miss the Parks Canada release choose a Moraine Lake and Lake Louise shuttle instead.


You can compare the two routes in our guide to the Moraine Lake shuttle versus a private tour, or review other options in our article on Banff and Moraine Lake shuttle alternatives.


How to Get to the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail Without a Car


Visiting without a rental car is entirely realistic. There are four main ways to do it.
‍

The first is the Parks Canada shuttle. It is the most affordable route, but it requires early booking, a trip to the Lake Louise Park and Ride and some flexibility around wait times.


The second is a commercial shuttle with hotel or town pickup. This suits travellers staying in Banff, Canmore or Lake Louise who want a simple round trip without managing reservations and parking. Vista Chase runs sunrise and golden hour shuttles to Moraine Lake and Lake Louise with pickup from Banff, Canmore and Lake Louise Village.

The third is a small-group tour. If you want to see Moraine Lake as part of a bigger day that includes Lake Louise, Emerald Lake and other highlights, our shared tours keep groups small and costs reasonable.


The fourth is a private tour. A private tour with a local guide lets you set the pace, stay as long as you like at the Rockpile and choose your own mix of stops. Our article on a VIP Moraine Lake private tour explains what that experience looks like in practice, and our guide on visiting Moraine Lake without a car covers the full range of choices in more depth.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail Free to Visit?


The trail itself does not have a separate fee. You are walking on public land within a national park, so there is no ticket for the Rockpile. Your costs come from the other parts of the trip: a Parks Canada day pass or Discovery Pass for park entry, plus your transport, whether that is a shuttle seat, a guided tour or another approved option.


Check the latest park fees and shuttle prices on the Parks Canada website before you go, because rates change from season to season. If you book with a guided operator, ask whether park fees are included. On Vista Chase tours, we handle timing, permits and Parks Canada fees as part of the service, which removes one of the most common first-timer headaches.


What Is the Best Time to Visit the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


The best time depends on what you want from the view.


Sunrise is the most dramatic. Early light can turn the peaks orange and pink and the lake is calm, which gives the best reflections. It is also the most competitive time for access, so book well ahead. Our Moraine Lake sunrise tours guide explains how access works at that hour.


Mid-morning is the best choice for colour. When the sun is higher, the lake shows its brightest turquoise, which is what most people picture when they imagine Moraine Lake. Late afternoon and golden hour bring softer light and often smaller crowds as day visitors head home.


By season, the lake colour is strongest from late June through September, when glacial meltwater carries rock flour into the water. In late September, golden larch trees add a second reason to visit, although the shuttle season may be ending around then. Winter and early spring access is limited and conditions are unpredictable, so confirm what is open before you plan.


For photographers, our seasonal guide to the best time to visit Moraine Lake for photos goes deeper on light and timing, and our comparison of Lake Louise sunrise versus sunset helps you decide how to pair the two lakes. If you are planning around autumn colour, see the best Banff tours for fall colors.


What Should You Bring for the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


The Rockpile is short, but mountain weather changes quickly, so pack for the environment rather than the distance.


Wear grippy walking shoes or light trail shoes. Bring a warm layer even in summer, because mornings at the lake are cold, and a light rain jacket for sudden showers. Carry water, a small snack, sunscreen and sunglasses, since the high-altitude sun is strong. A fully charged phone, or a camera with a spare battery, is essential because cold drains batteries faster than you expect. Bring your shuttle or tour confirmation as a printed copy or screenshot, since mobile signal can be unreliable in the valley.


If you want a full seasonal checklist, our Banff packing list by season covers everything from summer layers to winter gear.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail Worth Visiting?


Yes, and for most first-time visitors it is the single best return on effort in the Canadian Rockies. You do not need a full day of hiking to experience the view that made Moraine Lake famous. If you have limited time, an easy fitness level or children with you, the Rockpile delivers the headline moment with almost no strain.


It is also worth visiting for a quieter reason. Standing above the lake and seeing the peaks wrap around the water gives a sense of scale that photographs never fully capture. Travellers who want to compare it with its famous neighbour can read our guide on whether Lake Louise is worth visiting.


How to Visit the Rockpile Trail for the First Time: A Simple Plan


Start by choosing how you will reach Moraine Lake, because everything else depends on that decision. If you want the lowest cost and can book early, target the Parks Canada shuttle. If you want certainty, pickup and a smoother day, choose a commercial shuttle or a guided tour.


Next, pick your time slot. Choose sunrise for atmosphere and fewer people, or mid-morning for the strongest turquoise water. Then confirm the current season dates, weather and any road or trail advisories on the Parks Canada website.


On the day itself, arrive at the lake and head straight to the Rockpile before the crowd builds. Take your photos, then spend time on the lakeshore trail or the canoe dock. If your schedule allows, continue to Lake Louise for a second iconic view. Our one-day Lake Louise and Moraine Lake tour guide shows how to combine both lakes without rushing.


Common First-Timer Mistakes to Avoid


The most common mistake is assuming you can drive to the lake. The road is closed to personal vehicles, so arriving by car without a shuttle or tour booking leaves you stranded at the Lake Louise side.


The second is booking too late. Peak-season shuttle seats and sunrise tour spots can disappear weeks in advance, and our Banff tour booking tips explain how to avoid missing out.


The third is underestimating the cold and the crowds. Arrive layered, expect other visitors on the viewpoint and be patient while people take turns for photos. The fourth is leaving no buffer time. Shuttle waits, summit queues and photo stops all add up, so avoid scheduling tight connections after your Moraine Lake visit.


Who Should Choose a Private Tour, a Shared Tour or a Shuttle?


A shuttle suits independent travellers who only want transport to Moraine Lake and Lake Louise and prefer to explore alone. A shared small-group tour suits solo travellers, couples and budget-conscious visitors who want a guide and several stops in one day. A private tour suits families, photographers and anyone who values flexibility and a slower pace. Our comparison of private tours versus group tours in Banff walks through the trade-offs, and our guide on private tours versus public shuttles helps if transport is your main concern.


Travelling with children? Our family-friendly Banff tours guide explains how to build a comfortable day for all ages. If you are staying several days, a multi-day Rockies tour package can bundle airport transfers and daily touring so you never need a rental car.


Why Book the Rockpile Trail Visit With Vista Chase?


Vista Chase is a Banff-based tour operator offering private tours, shared small-group tours, shuttles and multi-day journeys across Banff, Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, Yoho and the Icefields Parkway. Our local guides handle timing, access and park fees so you can focus on the view. Learn more about our team on the About Us page, browse the photo gallery for a preview of what you will see, or visit our travel blog for more planning guides.


Ready to plan your day at Moraine Lake? Explore our private tours, compare our shared tours, reserve a shuttle or contact our team for help choosing the right option. You can also read answers to common questions on our FAQ page.


Frequently Asked Questions About the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail


Where is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail located?


It is at Moraine Lake in Banff National Park, Alberta, beside the lakeshore at the end of Moraine Lake Road, roughly 14 kilometres from Lake Louise Village.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail suitable for beginners?


Yes. It is a short, easy climb with steps and rocky footing, suitable for most first-time hikers and families with older children, though it is not accessible for wheelchairs or strollers.


How long does it take to hike the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


Most people complete the walk in 10 to 20 minutes each way, and about 20 to 30 minutes with time for photos at the top.


How difficult is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


It is rated easy, with minimal elevation gain. Wet or icy conditions can make the upper section slippery, so wear shoes with good grip.


What is the best time to visit the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


Sunrise offers the most dramatic light and calm water, while mid-morning in summer shows the brightest turquoise colour. Late June to September is the strongest season for lake colour.


Can you drive directly to Moraine Lake?


No. Moraine Lake Road is closed to personal vehicles year-round, with limited exceptions for licensed commercial operators, registered lodge guests and official vehicles.


Do you need a shuttle reservation to visit Moraine Lake?


You need a reservation for the Parks Canada shuttle. If you travel with a licensed commercial shuttle or tour operator, your booking covers access instead.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail free to visit?


The trail has no separate fee, but you still need park entry and a way to reach the lake, such as a shuttle seat or guided tour.


What should you bring for the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail?


Bring grippy shoes, warm layers, a rain jacket, water, snacks, sunscreen, a charged phone or camera and your booking confirmation saved offline.


Is the Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail worth visiting?


Yes. It is one of the easiest ways to see the most famous view in the Canadian Rockies, and it takes only a short time.


Final Thoughts


The Moraine Lake Rockpile Trail proves that a world-class view does not require a world-class hike. With a little planning around access, timing and weather, a first visit can be calm, rewarding and well organised. Decide how you will reach the lake, choose the light you want to photograph and let a local team take care of the logistics when it makes sense. Your view of the Valley of the Ten Peaks will be ready when you arrive.

Before you travel, always check the latest Parks Canada notices for shuttle dates, road status and trail conditions, since operating rules can change from season to season.
